prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Long, The, Train

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version:

---

Long before the train appears,
The tracks begin to sing and tremble;
Long before we know the direction
From which it comes, a distant hum
Announces its approach.

And so we drop upon all fours
Even before we glance to left or right.
We skip across the wooden sleepers
Or walk the rail, balanced and sure.

We speak of the capital,
Where the train concludes its journey
From the interior—laden with
The outsized trunks of felled trees
And open-topped cars brimming with bauxite.

We always hide from it, uncertain
What the train might do should we
Dare to stand beside the tracks.
It flattens our nails into knives;
It obliterates all traffic
Caught within its path at crossroads;
It whistles like a battle cry,
Its engine's steam a warning—
A mood not to be trifled with.

Rails without beginning or end,
Twinned hopes forever at your back,
Forever up ahead, urging you onward—
Double oxen, hoof-stomp, temper-
Tantrum, stampede, clatter-
Matter, head-splitter, hear us,
Stooped low with an ear against the line—

Greenheart, mora, baromalli,
Purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli, womara.

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone further, preserve the original line breaks more strictly, or refine any particular section?

Well before the train comes into view,
The rails begin to hum and shiver.
Well before you can tell which way
The train is heading, a droning sound
Warns you it will be here shortly.
This is why we drop down onto our hands and knees
Even before glancing to either side.
We hop between the wooden ties or move
Ahead by keeping steady on a single rail.
Our conversation turns to the city
Where the train's journey concludes,
Coming from the backcountry loaded with
Enormous logs of chopped-down
Trees and roofless wagons full of bauxite.
We always take cover from it, uncertain
Of how the train might react should we
Remain beside the tracks.
It presses our nails flat as blades,
It destroys whatever crosses its path
When it meets the road,
It shrieks like a war cry,
The engine's steam a temper
You wouldn't dare provoke.
Tracks with no start and no finish,
Paired hopes forever behind you,
Forever ahead, waving you onward,
Twin oxen, pounding hooves, a fit of
Rage, a wild rush, a rattling
Din, a skull cracker, listen to us,
Bent low with an ear against the line—
greenheart, mora, baromalli, purple heart, crabwood, kabakalli, womara.
outputs.L3:
# The Approaching Train

Long before the train becomes visible, long before anyone can tell which direction it will come from, it announces its own arrival. The sound travels ahead of it, and the vibration hums through the metal tracks, a signal that reaches those who know how to listen. The train speaks first through the ground itself.

The children have learned to read these signs. The moment they sense the tremor, they drop instinctively to all fours, pressing themselves close to the earth to feel the approach more fully. For them, the tracks are a place of play. They balance carefully along the narrow rails, testing their footing, and they leap from sleeper to sleeper, skipping across the wooden ties in a game that belongs entirely to them.

The train itself is bound for the capital, making its long journey from the interior of the country. Its cars are heavy with cargo drawn from the land: felled tree trunks stacked and chained, and loads of bauxite hauled from the earth to be carried toward the coast.

Yet the children fear this train, and their fear is not unfounded. It possesses a destructive power that flattens whatever lies in its path. It obliterates everything in its way, and its whistle cuts through the air like a battle cry, a warning and a threat announcing its unstoppable advance.

The poem draws to a close by naming the trees one by one, each species called out in turn. In doing so, it binds the timber that rides in the cars to the simple, intimate act of listening—an ear pressed low against the line, waiting to feel the distant train.
outputs.L4:
# The Approaching Train

Along the railway line, where the steel tracks stretch through the humid landscape, children have learned to read the language of the rails. Before any sound reaches their ears, before any shape appears on the horizon, they feel it—a subtle humming that vibrates through the metal, a faint trembling in the ground beneath their bare feet. This is their first warning, an instinctive knowledge passed down through play and repetition, teaching them when the great machine is coming.

They gather here often, drawn to the tracks as playgrounds despite the danger. There is a caution in their movements, a wariness bred into their games. They place their small hands against the cool steel to test for that telltale vibration, and when it comes, they scatter back to safety, watching from a respectful distance. Their play is punctuated by these moments of alertness, a rhythm of freedom and retreat dictated by the schedule of passing trains.

When the train finally emerges, it reveals its purpose. The children observe its cargo with curious eyes: felled trees stacked and bound, their trunks torn from the deep interior of the land, and heaps of bauxite—the reddish ore destined for distant refineries and foreign markets. This is the harvest of the forest and the earth, carried away on iron rails toward some unseen destination beyond the children's world.

The train itself commands both fascination and fear. It is portrayed as an overwhelming force, a mechanical beast of immense power. Nothing stands in its way; it could flatten any object caught upon the tracks, obliterate the ordinary flow of traffic and life that dares to cross its path. Its passage is absolute, unstoppable, a demonstration of industrial might cutting through the landscape with indifferent authority.

The poem closes with a list of native tree species—a naming of the specific trees that grow in this land, or perhaps that once grew here before the axes came. This catalogue of names serves a deeper purpose than mere description. It underscores the theme of extraction: the systematic removal of natural resources from the interior, the stripping of the forest, the transformation of living landscape into commodity. Each name is both a celebration of what exists and a quiet lament for what is being carried away, load by load, on the trembling rails the children have learned so carefully to fear.
outputs.L5:
*The Long Train*

There's something almost hypnotic about a long train stretching across the horizon. It moves with a steady, unhurried rhythm, its many cars linked together in an endless procession that seems to have no beginning and no end.

I remember standing at a railway crossing as a child, counting the cars as they rumbled past. The barrier would come down, the warning bells would ring, and then the great machine would appear. One car, two cars, ten, twenty—I'd lose count somewhere in the middle, mesmerized by the sheer length of it all.

The long train carries more than just cargo or passengers. It carries a sense of journey, of distance, of places far beyond where we stand. Each car might hold coal, grain, automobiles, or the dreams of travelers heading toward new lives. The train doesn't care about our impatience as we wait at the crossing; it simply continues on its way, connecting one point to another across the vast landscape.

There's a poetry in the way a long train travels through the night. Its headlight cuts through the darkness, and its whistle echoes across sleeping towns and empty fields. For those who hear it, the sound is both lonely and comforting—a reminder that somewhere, something is always moving, always heading somewhere.

The longer the train, the more it seems to embody patience and persistence. It cannot stop quickly, cannot turn sharply, cannot change its mind. It commits to its path and follows it faithfully, mile after mile, hour after hour. In this way, the long train teaches us something about determination and the beauty of staying the course.

And when the last car finally passes, and the barrier lifts, we continue on our own journeys—perhaps a little more thoughtful, having watched the long train disappear into the distance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem from the perspective of children in Guyana who play near railway tracks, waiting for a train that carries timber and bauxite from the interior.
counterfactuals.output:
Waiting by the Rails

We know the sound before we hear it—
the way the ground remembers,
the way the small stones
begin their trembling.

Mama says stay back
but the rails are warm
under our bare feet,
two long ribbons of silver
running into the green
that swallows everything—
the interior, they call it,
where the big trees fall
and the red earth gives up
its secret weight.

We press our ears down
the way our fathers taught us,
listening for the metal breath
coming from far,
from places we have only
named in school:
Mackenzie, Ituni, the deep places
where the men go
and come back smaller,
their hands the color of the bauxite,
orange-brown, ground into the lines
of their knuckles.

Here it comes now—
first the smell,
diesel and cut wood,
greenheart and mora
stacked like the bones
of giants,
then the great shaking,
the horn splitting the afternoon,
and we are running alongside,
we are shouting nothing,
we are only running,
waving at the man in the window
who never waves back
but is not unkind,
only tired,
only carrying the whole country
out toward the coast
on his slow iron shoulders.

And then it is gone.
The last car
drags its long shadow
after it,
and the rails hum down
to nothing,
and the stones lie still again,
and we stand
in the settling dust,
small along the empty line,

already listening
for the next one,
already believing
the train will bring us back
whatever it has taken—
the trees, the fathers,
the red weight of the ground—
though we are young enough
to still believe this,
and the tracks
stretch on
in both directions,
shining,
saying nothing,
going where we have not yet
been allowed to follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem about the sound and menace of an approaching train, ending with a list of tropical hardwood names.
counterfactuals.output:
**Approach**

First a tremor in the rail,
a rumor running down the steel,
faint as breath, then hard as hail—
the ground begins to feel.

Now the low note in the wood
of ties that shudder, one by one,
a bass that thrums where trestles stood
before the sound had come.

It gathers weight. It hoards the dark.
It swallows crickets, wind, and gnat.
The whistle tears a ragged mark
across the flatland's flat.

Louder—louder—now the roar
is teeth and iron, wheel and wrath,
a hundred tons and then some more
come howling down the path.

The crossing bells go frantic-bright,
the air is hammered, split, and thrown,
and everything within its sight
is shaken to the bone—

then thunder, thunder, thunder past,
a wall of wind, a blur, a scream,
the whole world rattling, holding fast
against the passing dream.

And in the after-ringing hush,
when steel has drained back into steel,
I list the woods the freight might crush,
the cargo in its keel:

mahogany, teak,
ipe, purpleheart,
rosewood, ebony,
cocobolo, wenge,
zebrawood, bloodwood,
padauk, iroko,
jatoba, cumaru,
tigerwood, greenheart—

each name a plank, a grain, a ghost
of forests loud as any train,
now silent, riding coast to coast,
and gone into the rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about anticipation and railroads, where the tracks themselves seem alive—singing, trembling, warning of the train's arrival.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rails Speak First

Before the whistle, before the light,
the iron knows what's coming.

Lay your palm against the steel—
feel it hum, a low electric prayer,
the far-off weight of something
gathering in the distance,
riding the long cold spine of the line
toward this exact and waiting place.

The tracks are never silent.
They sing in frequencies
the body understands before the mind,
a trembling in the ties,
a shiver climbing up through gravel,
through the soles of your shoes,
into the hollow of your chest.

*It comes,* they say. *It comes.*

The rails go taut as fiddle strings,
each rivet holding its breath,
each spike a note held down
beneath the thunder still unseen—
and the whole earth leans forward,
listening,
the way you lean when someone speaks
a name you've waited years to hear.

Now the singing sharpens.
Now the metal cries aloud,
warning the sleepers, warning the crows,
warning the small bones in your ankles:
*step back, step back, it's almost here,
the future with its blazing eye
and its unstoppable song.*

And then—the light.
And then—the wind that isn't wind
but the sheer displacement of arrival,
the world made suddenly loud and gold
and gone.

The rails still ring
long after,
holding the memory of motion
like a struck bell,
already trembling,
already listening
for the next.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid poem exploring how a train dominates a landscape and the imagination of those who watch it, incorporating imagery of logging and mining.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Iron Passage

Across the valley's ancient spine
it comes—a serpent forged in fire,
its breath a smoke-and-cinder line
drawn hard against the timber's choir.

The mountains lean to watch it pass,
those slopes once thick with standing pine
now stripped to stumps and yellowed grass
where axe and saw have drawn their line.

It hauls the forest's fallen dead,
whole cathedrals stacked and bound,
the cedar's red, the fir's dark thread,
their green cathedral come to ground.

And children on the trestle's edge
grow still as prophets at the sight—
they read the future in its wedge
of thunder splitting open light.

It carries copper, coal, and ore,
the mountain's dark and secret blood
torn upward from the bedrock floor
and rolled away in rust and mud.

The old men lean on fences, dreaming
of somewhere down that vanished track,
their whole horizon turned to steaming
distance that won't bring them back.

The landscape bends beneath its weight—
the river startles, cattle turn—
this god of schedule, steel, and freight
that teaches valleys how to yearn.

And when it's gone, the silence rings
with something emptied, something changed:
the stumps, the shafts, the hollowed things,
a country permanently rearranged.

Yet still we watch. Still something calls
from that long whistle's fading cry—
the way it conquers, claims, and hauls
our small lives with it, rolling by.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical poem that begins "Long before you see train / The tracks sing and tremble" and closes with the names of Guyanese trees like greenheart and purpleheart.
counterfactuals.output:
**Long Before You See the Train**

Long before you see train
the tracks sing and tremble,
a low hum walking the iron,
a shiver run down the sleepers,
and the bush hold its breath.

You feel it in your soles first,
then your teeth, then your chest—
that far-off engine dragging
its cargo of morning through the green,
whistle folded in the distance
like a bird you cannot name.

The old ones knew this sound.
They set their ears to the ground
the way a mother sets her palm
against a fevered brow,
reading the coming of things
in a music before music,
in the earth's slow warning.

And when it passes—God, the roar,
the wind of it, the smoke,
the whole savannah leaning—
then quiet folds back down
soft as a kiskadee settling,
and you are left standing
where the rails still whisper
long after the last car has gone.

So let the train remember me
when I am only trembling too,
a rumor in the roots, a song
gone underground and traveling.
Bury me among the giants
that outlast every whistle,
that stood before the iron came
and stand there after:

mora and wallaba,
crabwood, locust, silverballi—
and deep in that dark heartwood,
harder than sorrow, holding,
the greenheart and the purpleheart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
